Multilevel simulations demonstrate single-qubit gate fidelities above $99.99\%$; the simpler protocol remains robust under moderate variations of qubit parameters and flux bias, while the combined protocol preserves high fidelity while substantially accelerating the gate. These results establish SFQ-based cryogenic control as a realistic route to fast, accurate, and scalable manipulation of fluxonium qubits.

Quantum Physics.title: Dynamical Casimir emission from Floquet-driven Landau polaritons: Gauge invariance forbids a superradiant phase transition
Quantum Physics.summary: Ultrastrong light--matter coupling of linear systems, such as Landau polaritons formed by a two-dimensional electron gas in a terahertz cavity, is described by the bosonic Hopfield model, and gauge invariance forbids a superradiant phase transition (SRPT). Modulating the magnetic field alone has been predicted to enhance the cycle-averaged coupling and induce a Floquet SRPT. We develop an exact theory of periodically driven Landau polaritons. Including the electric field induced by the modulated flux (Faraday's law), the problem reduces exactly, by Kohn's theorem, to the electronic center-of-mass mode coupled to the cavity, whose Hamiltonian is a sum of squares at every instant. A theorem of Krein then guarantees stability to all orders above a computable drive frequency, the Krein frequency, for which we give a self-contained proof. Below it, the system is stable except within resonance tongues where the drive creates pairs from the vacuum, the dynamical Casimir effect. At high drive frequency the electrons experience the mean field plus a ponderomotive trap (the Fock--Darwin problem), not an enhanced coupling. A gauge theorem excludes a Floquet photon condensate for any band structure, including Kane nonparabolicity, for which we derive a generalized Thomas--Reiche--Kuhn (TRK) sum rule. The predicted transition arises from averaging the coupling in a fixed Landau-level basis, which yields an effective model that violates the TRK sum rule; under driving, gauge invariance also requires the induced Faraday field. The rule to modulate and average the minimal-coupling Hamiltonian, not the parameters of its projection, applies to any linear, minimally coupled system. Instead of an SRPT, magnetic modulation produces dynamical Casimir emission: Faraday-driven polariton--magnetoplasmon pairs at low threshold, and two-color photon pairs with up to 5--10~dB of two-mode squeezing.

Quantum Physics.title: Below-shot-noise capacity in phase estimation using nonlinear interferometers
Quantum Physics.summary: Over the past decade, several schemes for imaging and sensing based on nonlinear interferometers have been proposed and demonstrated experimentally. These interferometers exhibit two main advantages. First, they enable probing a sample at a chosen wavelength while detecting light at a different wavelength with high efficiency (bicolor quantum imaging and sensing with undetected light). Second, they can show quantum-enhanced sensitivities below the shot-noise limit, potentially reaching Heisenberg-limited precision in parameter estimation. Here, we compare three quantum-imaging configurations using only easily accessible intensity-based measurements for phase estimation: a Yurke-type SU(1,1) interferometer, a Mandel-type induced-coherence interferometer, and a hybrid scheme that continuously interpolates between them. While an ideal Yurke interferometer can exhibit Heisenberg scaling, this advantage is known to be fragile under realistic detection constraints and in the presence of loss. We demonstrate that differential intensity detection in the Mandel interferometer provides the highest and most robust phase sensitivity among the considered schemes, reaching but not surpassing the shot-noise limit, even in the presence of loss. Intensity measurements in a Yurke-type configuration can achieve genuine sub-shot-noise sensitivity under balanced losses and moderate gain; however, their performance degrades in realistic high-gain regimes. Consequently, in this regime, the Mandel configuration with differential detection outperforms the Yurke-type setup and constitutes the most robust approach for phase estimation.
Quantum Physics.comment: 17 pages, 6 figures, all data and code required to reproduce the figures presented in this paper are publicly available in an online repository at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21703011, based on https://github.com/Cristofero1/below-shot-noise-phase-estimation

Quantum Physics.title: A New Computational Model for the Spin-Free Sum-of-Squares Energy Bounds of Electronic Hamiltonian
Quantum Physics.summary: Optimizing spin-free sum-of-squares (SOS) energy bounds for electronic Hamiltonians leads to semidefinite programs whose expanded size grows rapidly with the orbital dimension. We derive an exact reformulation of an established spin-free SOS model as a convex quadratic problem over a single symmetric matrix constrained between zero and the identity. Explicit recovery maps connect feasible quadratic-program iterates to certificates in the original SOS formulation, and identify the Frank--Wolfe gap with the separation between recovered primal and dual objectives. We implement the quadratic action through GPU-accelerated Coulomb contractions and solve the reformulated problem using a cached implementation of fully corrective Frank--Wolfe, referred to here as the dimension-reduced simplicial method (DRSM) that caches operator products and optimizes convex-combination weights in a small corrective quadratic program. Numerical experiments cover 65 FCIDUMP models, molecular geometries, and regular hydrogen rings, including original-coordinate recovery checks on nine instances and comparisons with FISTA and a boundary-point SDP solver. On eight H100 GPUs, a cold-start calculation for C$_{720}$ with 10,080 spatial orbitals reaches a freshly recomputed Frank--Wolfe gap of $8.82\times10^{-9}$ hartree in 5.02 hours. Full-space hydrogen-ring calculations reach 10,000 orbitals, with cyclic reduction providing further computational savings. These results show how exact reformulation, data structure exploitation and reuse of Coulomb actions make optimization of the selected large-scale SOS relaxation practical.
Quantum Physics.comment: 35 pages, 2 figures. Yuming Bao and Yancheng Wu contributed equally to this work and share first authorship

Quantum Physics.title: Error Resilience and Unitary 2-Designs
Quantum Physics.summary: Encoding-error-decoding circuits provide a setting for studying protection of quantum information against errors. In these circuits, an encoding unitary is followed by an error layer, decoding by the inverse unitary, and ancilla postselection. For encoders drawn from unitary 2-design ensembles, these circuits exhibit an error-protecting phase below a threshold error strength in which the fidelity between the input and recovered logical states approaches unity. Here, we show how departures from Haar second-moment statistics of the encoder can destabilize the error-protecting phase and derive a universal inequality linking recovery fidelity to the second unitary frame potential, which quantifies the ensemble's proximity to a unitary 2-design. This connection is exemplified by matchgate circuits doped with a tunable number of non-Gaussian gates. We analytically show that undoped circuits lack a stable error-protecting phase in the thermodynamic limit and that increasing the doping restores the error protection mechanism as the encoder ensemble approaches an approximate unitary 2-design. Further examples of Hamiltonian encoders, including an experimentally motivated all-to-all spin model, follow the same mechanism. Our results identify recovery fidelity as a diagnostic of departures from unitary 2-design behavior in quantum many-body systems.

Quantum Physics.title: Electrical Stark Tuning and In Situ Field Sensing of $V_{2}$ Silicon Vacancies in a 4H-SiC a-Plane Lateral pin-Diode
Quantum Physics.summary: Silicon carbide has emerged as a highly promising platform for scalable quantum technologies, with the silicon vacancy serving as a robust spin qubit and quantum sensor. However, conventional c-plane 4H-SiC restricts the experimental scheme and resonant optical excitation to the sample's geometry. The usage of a-plane substrates enables more versatile resonant optical access to the color center through the wafer surface. Here, we demonstrate the electrical control and optical addressability of $V_{2}$ (cubic lattice site) silicon vacancies within the intrinsic region of lateral pin-diodes fabricated on a-plane 4H-SiC wafers using a scalable complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) process. Despite extensive semiconductor processing, the integrated color centers exhibit good optical quality, evidenced by narrow optical transition linewidths below 80 MHz at zero bias. These embedded quantum sensors are utilized for in situ measurement of local electric fields at cryogenic temperatures via the Stark effect. Comparisons with macroscopic technology computer-aided design simulations reveal the value of these integrated quantum sensors to help understand cryogenic device behavior, for example in predicting highly localized field crowding. Furthermore, to address the spectral indistinguishability required for quantum networks, we precisely tune the zero-phonon line (ZPL) of individual emitters via the reverse-bias Stark effect. This successfully compensates for the spectral variations of distinct emitters. Following the relaxation of transient charge fluctuations, the Stark-tuned emitters exhibit spectral stability over measurement periods exceeding four hours. Our results establish a-plane 4H-SiC as a robust platform for future interference experiments and quantum photonic integrated circuits.

Quantum Physics.title: Reading long-range information from a separable quantum record requires entangled measurements
Quantum Physics.summary: Qubit probes record the relative orientation of neighboring, initially uncorrelated Ising spins through local interactions. Each probe encodes one bond label in two states with overlap $1-p$. The resulting probe record is fully separable. A receiver gets one copy and guesses whether two distant spins point in the same or opposite directions. On the square lattice, the best readout with separable measurement effects approaches success probability $1/2$ as the spin separation grows, for $0<p\le p_0=1-1/\sqrt2$. This includes all local operations with classical communication. The same conclusion holds for every measurement whose effects remain positive under partial transposition across every cut of the probes. For $p_*=0.29181\le p\le1$, a joint readout of the same record maintains a success probability above $1/2$ by a positive amount independent of distance. The overlap $[p_*,p_0]$ gives a strict separation between the readouts. A record that is created locally and contains no entanglement can therefore hold long-range information that only measurements with entangled effects can read.

Quantum Physics.title: Random encoders and expurgation improve 1,873 entries of the Grassl qubit code tables
Quantum Physics.summary: I report 192 explicit binary stabilizer codes $[[n,k,d]]$ with $53\le n\le 254$ and $5\le d\le 13$ whose minimum distance exceeds the lower bound listed in Grassl's code tables at the same $(n,k)$: 161 codes by one and 31 by two. Through the standard propagation rules they raise 1,873 entries of the table. For 190 of the codes, a random Clifford encoder is followed by expurgation: every logical operator of weight below the target distance is enumerated, and a few logical operators are promoted to stabilizers so that each low-weight one anticommutes with at least one of them. The other two are obtained by puncturing a code from the table and repairing it in the same way. All 192 distances are exact: the lower bound is certified by exhaustive meet-in-the-middle enumeration of up to $4\times10^{13}$ Pauli operators, and the upper bound by an explicit logical operator of weight $d$. A first-moment count explains the results. Expurgated random codes have about eight more logical qubits than a typical random code of the same length and distance, so they beat the table wherever its best known codes are no better than random. The largest gains, up to nine logical qubits, are at $d\ge9$ and $n\gtrsim170$, where the table often gives a lower bound without an explicit code. The same count predicts improvements at 619 further pairs $(n,d)$. The search was run by AI agents. The codes, their certificates and an independent checker are public.
Quantum Physics.comment: 6 pages, 1 figure; codes and data at https://github.com/MarinAndreGirard/qubit-stabilizer-codes-2026

Quantum Physics.title: Edge quantum weight of finite Chern flakes and its topological floor
Quantum Physics.summary: The zero-point energy of a circuit measures the polarization fluctuation of an insulator coupled to it. In a crystal this is the bulk quantum weight $K_\mathrm{bulk}$, which the Chern number $C$ bounds below by $|C|$. We show that a finite Chern flake adds an edge term that survives as the flake grows. The low-frequency transitions of its chiral edge carry a dipole weight, the sum of their squared dipole matrix elements, $K_\mathrm{edge}\geq|C|$ per unit area, a floor that follows from the positive absorption of both circular polarizations by every transition and the known cancellation of circular dichroism between edge and bulk. A weakly coupled circuit slower than the edge modes therefore reads $K_\mathrm{bulk}+K_\mathrm{edge}$, averaged over two field directions, while a faster one below the bulk gap approaches $K_\mathrm{bulk}$, so which quantum weight is measured depends on whether the flake is made large or the circuit slow first. Exact free-fermion calculations on lattice flakes bear out the floor and this dependence on the circuit frequency. The result holds at weak coupling, which a growing flake at fixed coupling eventually leaves. Above the floor, the edge weight of one channel is a number fixed by the shape of the boundary and the edge velocities, which square and rectangular lattice flakes follow to within 0.003. Each further edge channel adds its own such number, while the circular dichroism of the edge counts only the net chirality.
Quantum Physics.comment: 39 pages, 13 figures. Data and code: doi:10.5281/zenodo.24112974

Quantum Physics.title: Optimal Calibration of Qubit Detuning and Crosstalk
Quantum Physics.summary: Characterizing and calibrating physical qubits is essential for maintaining the performance of quantum processors. A key challenge in this process is the presence of crosstalk that complicates the estimation of individual qubit detunings. In this work, we derive optimal strategies for estimating detuning and crosstalk parameters by optimizing Ramsey interference experiments using Fisher information and the Cramer-Rao bound. We compare several calibration protocols, including measurements of a single quadrature at multiple times and of two quadratures at a single time, for a fixed number of total measurements. Our results predict that the latter approach yields the highest precision and robustness in both cases of isolated and coupled qubits. We validate experimentally our approach using a single NV center as well as superconducting transmons. Our approach enables accurate parameter extraction with significantly fewer measurements, resulting in up to a 50% reduction in calibration time while maintaining estimation accuracy.

Quantum Physics.title: Toric codes all the way down: decoupling translation-invariant topological CSS codes in higher dimensions
Quantum Physics.summary: Topological Calderbank-Shor-Steane (CSS) codes in more than two spatial dimensions offer features useful for fault-tolerant quantum computation, such as transversal non-Clifford gates and single-shot decoding, but a systematic understanding of them is still lacking. One approach is to decouple a code: map it to a stack of higher-form toric codes by a finite-depth local CSS-preserving Clifford circuit, possibly after adding ancillas. For translation-invariant $p$-ary CSS codes, where $p$ is prime ($p=2$ for qubits), we require the circuit to commute with the translations of a superlattice. In two dimensions, such a decoupling exists once these translations act trivially on every anyon type. In higher dimensions, excitations are sorted by their dimension into superselection layers, which can remain glued together even when translations act trivially on each layer. We show that this gluing is the only remaining obstruction: a code can be decoupled on a superlattice exactly when, after coarse-graining to it, translations act trivially on every layer and the gluing vanishes. Moreover, for a code with finitely many excitation types in each layer and $m$ nonzero layers, once translations act trivially on every layer, further coarse-graining by a factor of $p^{m-1}$ in every direction removes the aforementioned gluing. Physically, the same criterion determines when the code encodes the maximal number of logical qudits on a finite torus. Finally, we give an explicit algorithm that constructs the decoupling as a circuit of SUM (qudit CNOT) and SWAP gates.
Quantum Physics.comment: 22 pages, 4 figures. Code: https://github.com/hmx21/css-decoupling ; Lean formalization: https://github.com/hmx21/css-decoupling-lean . v2: references added, Zenodo DOIs added, minor edits . v3: references added, minor edits

Quantum Physics.title: A New Quantum Linear System Algorithm Beyond the Condition Number and Its Application to Solving Multivariate Polynomial Systems
Quantum Physics.summary:
Given a matrix $A$ of dimension $M \times N$ and a vector $\vec{b}$, the quantum linear system (QLS) problem asks for the preparation of a quantum state $|\vec{y}\rangle$ proportional to the solution of $A\vec{y} = \vec{b}$. Existing QLS algorithms have runtimes that scale linearly with the condition number $κ(A)$, the sparsity of $A$, and logarithmically with inverse precision, but often overlook structural properties of $\vec{b}$, whose alignment with $A$'s eigenspaces can greatly affect performance.
  In this work, we present a new QLS algorithm that explicitly leverages the structure of the right-hand side vector $\vec{b}$. The runtime of our algorithm depends polynomially on the sparsity of the augmented matrix $H = [A, -\vec{b}]$, the inverse precision, the $\ell_2$ norm of the solution $\vec{y} = A^+ \vec{b}$, and a new instance-dependent parameter \[ ET= \sum_{i=1}^M p_i^2 \cdot d_i, \] where $\vec{p} = (AA^{\top})^+ \vec{b}$, and $d_i$ denotes the squared $\ell_2$ norm of the $i$-th row of $H$. We also introduce a structure-aware rescaling technique tailored to the solution $\vec{y} = A^+ \vec{b}$. Unlike left preconditioning methods, which transform the linear system to $DA\vec{y} = D\vec{b}$, our approach applies a right rescaling matrix, reformulating the linear system as $AD\vec{z} = \vec{b}$.
  As an application of our instance-aware QLS algorithm and new rescaling scheme, we develop a quantum algorithm for solving multivariate polynomial systems in regimes where prior QLS-based methods fail. This yields an end-to-end framework applicable to a broad class of problems. In particular, we apply it to the maximum independent set (MIS) problem, formulated as a special case of a polynomial system, and show through detailed analysis that, under certain conditions, our quantum algorithm for MIS runs in polynomial time.

Quantum Physics.title: Flux-Activated Resonant Control of a Bosonic Quantum Memory
Quantum Physics.summary: Universal control of bosonic degrees of freedom provides a hardware-efficient route for quantum information processing with high-dimensional systems. Bosonic circuit quantum electrodynamics (cQED), which leverages auxillary transmons to coherently control long-lived superconducting cavities, is well suited to this goal. However, such systems are traditionally operated in the dispersive regime, where the nearly degenerate cavity transitions prohibit the direct addressability of individual excitation levels of the bosonic mode and increase gate complexity. Here, we achieve direct oscillator control by dynamically accessing the resonant Jaynes-Cummings (JC) interactions, implemented with a hardware that integrates on-chip broadband magnetic flux delivery with a bosonic memory housed in a 3D superconducting cavity with lifetime exceeding 0.5 ms. We demonstrate deterministic preparation of Fock states and their superpositions within 100s of nanoseconds by directly climbing the JC ladder, and realise efficient arbitrary rotations between a pair of Fock states. Our resonant control scheme provides an analytical method for manipulating the entire Hilbert space of the bosonic mode at rates potentially more favourable than traditional dispersive strategies. This on-demand access to JC interactions serves as a foundational demonstration of an alternative strategy toward realising robust Fock-basis qudits and harnessing the rich dynamics of high-dimensional bosonic systems for quantum information processing.
Quantum Physics.comment: 28 pages, 15 figures; main text 5 pages, 4 figures

Quantum Physics.title: Classical phase unwrapping enables large-time-step unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization
Quantum Physics.summary: For computing molecular energies on early fault-tolerant hardware, unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization (UQKSD) avoids both the deep circuits of quantum phase estimation and the Pauli-term sampling of variational methods by extracting the energies from a projected real-time propagator. At a small time step $τ$, nearly linearly dependent Krylov vectors make the overlap matrix ill-conditioned. Our tests at fixed total evolution time show that additional Krylov vectors then add no accuracy, while the thresholded energy becomes increasingly sensitive to the choice of cutoff. A larger time step improves the conditioning and reduces the Krylov dimension $M$ needed for a target accuracy, but the energies are then known only modulo $2π/τ$. We present Classical Unwrapping for Resolving Eigenvalues (CURE-QKSD), a classical post-processing method that leaves the UQKSD circuits and generalized eigenvalue problem unchanged and recovers the missing multiples of $2π/τ$ from phase-consistency landscapes of one or, when needed, two UQKSD runs. In noiseless tests on six molecules with 12--20 qubits, all 28 targeted energies are recovered in their aliased regimes with final errors of at most $1.1\times10^{-7}$~Ha. Under Gaussian noise with $σ=10^{-4}$, the median error of the ground or first excited state reaches chemical accuracy at large aliased time steps with $M=20$--$65$, whereas uncorrected principal-branch energies are off by $0.7$--$115$~Ha. CURE-QKSD therefore makes aliased time steps usable for UQKSD calculations with smaller, better-conditioned Krylov bases.

Quantum Physics.title: Barriers to dequantization of near-term molecular electronic structure methods
Quantum Physics.summary: We prove classical simulation hardness, under the generalized $\mathsf{P}\neq\mathsf{NP}$ conjecture, for quantum circuit families with applications in near-term molecular electronic ground and excited state estimation. The proof exploits a connection to particle number conserving matchgate circuits with fermionic magic state inputs, which are shown to be universal for quantum computation under postselection, and are therefore not classically simulable in the worst case, in either the strong (multiplicative) or weak (sampling) sense. We apply these results to non-orthogonal quantum eigensolvers designed for near-term hardware by ruling out sample-based dequantization strategies to additively approximate the off-diagonal matrix elements between orbital-rotated correlated reference states that satisfy an irreducible fermionic magic property, which combines anticoncentration in any orbital basis with an average-case multiplicative approximation hardness conjecture for the associated matrix polynomials. We apply this complexity analysis to two choices of ansatz that incorporate both static and dynamic correlations to model the electronic eigenstates of molecular systems. These are linear combinations of orbital-rotated matrix product states, which are preparable in linear depth, and linear combinations of states prepared by generalized unitary coupled cluster with singles and doubles or unitary cluster Jastrow circuits of polynomial depth, for which computing the expectation values of local fermionic observables up to a constant additive error is $\mathsf{BQP}$-complete. We discuss the implications for achieving practical quantum advantage in resolving the electronic structure of catalytic systems composed from multivalent transition metal atoms using near-term quantum hardware.

Quantum Physics.title: Disorder-Induced Logarithmic Spreading and Localization of Quantum Fluctuations
Quantum Physics.summary: Disorder can localize quantum particles, even in the presence of interactions, but its influence on quantum fluctuations beyond mean--field dynamics remains poorly understood. Here, we investigate the propagation of quantum fluctuations in weakly interacting disordered bosonic systems by comparing the Bose--Hubbard model with the Gross--Pitaevskii equation. We find that, in contrast to ballistic spreading in the disorder--free system, quantum fluctuations exhibit logarithmic spreading at intermediate times under both random and quasiperiodic disorder, before eventually saturating. The spreading rate decreases algebraically with increasing disorder strength, and this behavior persists across different particle numbers and extends to two dimensions. Using a time--dependent Bogoliubov--de Gennes framework, we identify the localized mean--field wavefunction as a time--dependent pairing background that generates quantum fluctuations. The exponential suppression of fluctuation--generation rates with distance provides a physical mechanism for the logarithmically advancing fluctuation front. Our results reveal a distinct regime of disorder--controlled quantum--fluctuation dynamics and establish disorder as a means of controlling their spreading.

Quantum Physics.title: Floquet mobility edges and transport in a periodically driven generalized Aubry-André model
Quantum Physics.summary: We investigate the effect of a periodic electric field drive on the generalized Aubry-André model, also known as the Ganeshan-Pixley-Das Sarma (GPD) model, which is well known as a host of mobility edges. Our study of the Floquet spectrum of the driven GPD model uncovers the emergence of two distinct Floquet mobility edges, a delocalized--localized (DL) edge in the bounded regime, and a multifractal--localized (ML) edge in the unbounded regime. By mapping the high-frequency effective Hamiltonian to the static GPD model via a Bessel-renormalized hopping, the driven mobility edge formulae follow directly, with drive-induced localization arising naturally at specific values of the driving parameters, where the effective tunneling is coherently suppressed. Combined with numerical diagnostics such as the fractal dimension and inverse participation ratio, we demonstrate that these mobility edges can be effectively controlled by the amplitude and frequency of the electric field drive. Furthermore, the dynamical study of the periodically driven GPD model demonstrates superdiffusive to almost ballistic transport in the bounded regime corresponding to the DL edges, whereas subdiffusive transport is observed in the unbounded regime associated with the ML edges. We also analyze deviations from the high-frequency effective description by explicitly examining the low-frequency driving regime, where significant and counterintuitive deviations in both spectral properties and transport behavior are observed. Our study highlights the interplay of a quasiperiodic potential and a periodically varying electric field drive as a powerful mechanism to engineer mobility edges and control transport in systems with rich spectral features.

Quantum Physics.title: Low-energy spectral-window truncation for compact U(1) lattice gauge theory
Quantum Physics.summary: We prove a nonasymptotic electric-flux truncation bound for the entire vacuum-relative low-energy window of the original pure compact $U(1)$ lattice Hamiltonian. On a three-dimensional periodic cubic lattice with $N\geq3$ sites per direction at $θ=0$, in the gauge-invariant zero-global-flux sector, the factorial-squared tail-norm estimate holds for every normalized vector in the window, without physical eigenvalue-isolation, window-edge gap, or nondegeneracy assumptions and without a window-dimension factor. It controls finite-time hard-wall evolution from the normalized projection of the same initial state. An analytic finite-volume strong-coupling example in this model certifies a nonvacuum band and an order-one plaquette signal change preserved by a specified finite cutoff. The same estimate yields precision-dependent sufficient cutoffs, an alternative linear isometric encoding by polar decomposition for reference-entangled inputs, and local electric-square readout bounds. At fixed positive bare coupling, physical volume, window width, and duration, cutoffs scaling as $β\log N/\log\log N$ with $β>2$ make state and bounded-readout truncation errors vanish under lattice refinement.
Quantum Physics.comment: 21 pages, 1 table. Exact-arithmetic code and reference output included as ancillary files

Quantum Physics.title: Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization for Bounded-Payoff Imperfect-Information Games
Quantum Physics.summary: Imperfect-information games with a graded-reward structure present significant computational challenges for equilibrium computation, since the payoff expectations must be estimated across exponentially large strategy spaces. Counterfactual Regret Minimization over the years has proven effective for approximating Nash equilibria, but Monte Carlo variants create a large overhead of sampling costs when the counterfactual values are estimated from sampled game-tree trajectories. We propose a novel Quantum-Assisted Counterfactual Regret Minimization, a framework that uses Quantum Amplitude Estimation to reduce the computational complexity of the regret updates in bounded-payoff imperfect-information games, while preserving the convergence of its classical counterpart. We give a theoretical analysis of the resulting exploitability bound, discuss NISQ-compatible amplitude-estimation variants, the structure of their resource requirements, and outline what is needed to validate the potential advantage empirically.

Quantum Physics.title: Quantum-Informed Graph Decomposition
Quantum Physics.summary: The Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) is a near-term quantum algorithm for solving combinatorial optimization problems, but its accuracy and resource requirements may scale poorly with problem size or structure, reducing its utility in practice. Approaches such as the Graph Decomposition for Optimization Algorithm (GDOA) seek to address this by iteratively reducing an input problem until it reaches a size where it can be solved using QAOA while maintaining the same optimal solution. This algorithm, however, requires solving integer programs that have exponentially many variables, and can result in suboptimal solutions, as the integer programs may contain slack terms. In this work, we propose a heuristic called the Quantum Enhanced Graph Decomposition (QEGD) algorithm. Its novelty lies in its use of QAOA as a subroutine for sparsifying a graph through local vertex-merging. The algorithm, when used to sparsify MaxCut problems that are then solved using QAOA, achieves higher approximation ratios across all tested graphs than GDOA for random 5-regular and 6-regular graphs. We then compare the time-to-solution and approximation ratio of QEGD to other QAOA variants a collection of Erdös-Rényi graphs. QEGD has higher approximation ratios on average than QAOA$^2$ and ParaQAOA on all tested graphs. It also results in higher average approximation ratios than DC-QAOA on sparse Erdös-Rényi graphs and comparable average approximation ratio on denser Erdös-Rényi graphs. However, its average wall-clock time is between 0.4\% and 5\% of the average DC-QAOA wall-clock time.

Quantum Physics.title: Quantum-Enhanced QSAR for DYRK1A: Evaluating Complementary and Utility QPU-Derived Molecular Representations
Quantum Physics.summary: In drug discovery, hit identification selects a limited set of compounds for experimental evaluation from a larger collection of candidates. Because laboratory screening capacity is limited, that choice determines which chemical series continue into further investigation. A hit that is not assayed does not enter confirmation or the analog series, and that chemical series is not opened. For the DYRK1A kinase, the same test molecules were scored from a tabular representation of molecular descriptors and from a vector measured on a quantum processor, with the same RBF-SVM. The question is whether the two models propose the same set for experimental evaluation: they propose different compounds. The model on the vector measured on the quantum processor includes compounds that the tabular representation leaves out, and among them are already-labeled actives. The tabular representation includes actives that the vector measured on the quantum processor leaves out. What is reported is that set: who enters, with what label, and whether published chemistry already mentions it. No formal quantum advantage is claimed, nor a mechanism for why the two vectors separate differently. Those compounds fall within the neighborhood that both representations already cover; what changes is which model marks them active. From that follows the cost of predictive disagreement: each model would send a different chemical series to experimental evaluation.

Quantum Physics.title: Quantum Advantage in Assisted Work Distillation from Complementary Correlations
Quantum Physics.summary: We establish an operational bridge between microscale thermodynamic work extraction and the foundational characterization of nonclassical correlations in bipartite quantum systems. Within the resource theory of thermal operations, we analyze a generalized framework of assisted work distillation where the trusted receiver's system is divided into separate, independent particle storage pools. We demonstrate that concurrent information-theoretic correlations measured across sets of mutually unbiased bases act as an explicit, quantifiable energy resource for local work extraction. Based on this paradigm, we derive a novel class of work-based Einstein-Podolsky-Rosen steering inequalities whose violations certify a one-sided device-independent quantum thermodynamic enhancement. Furthermore, by restricting the dimension of the untrusted party under a one-sided semi-device-independent trust framework, we introduce dynamically scaling work inequalities capable of witnessing superunsteerability. This allows us to activate and certify the hidden thermodynamic utility of weakly correlated entangled states that are otherwise completely invisible in standard, unconstrained scenarios.

Quantum Physics.title: Computational complexity of Berry phase estimation in topological phases of matter
Quantum Physics.summary: The Berry phase is a fundamental quantity in the classification of topological phases of matter. In this paper, we present a new quantum algorithm and several complexity-theoretical results for the Berry phase estimation (BPE) problems. Our new quantum algorithm achieves BPE in a more general setting than previously known quantum algorithms, with a theoretical guarantee. For the complexity-theoretic results, we consider two main cases. First, we prove $\mathsf{BQP}$-completeness when we are given a guiding state that has a large overlap with the ground state. This result establishes an exponential quantum speedup for estimating the Berry phase. Second, we prove $\mathsf{UQMA} \cap \mathsf{co}$-$\mathsf{UQMA}$-completeness when we have an $\textit{a priori}$ bound for the ground-state energy. Here, $\mathsf{UQMA}$ is the unique witness version of $\mathsf{QMA}$, and $\mathsf{UQMA} \cap \mathsf{co}$-$\mathsf{UQMA}$ precisely captures the complexity of BPE without the known guiding state. Remarkably, this problem is, to our knowledge, the first natural problem complete for $\mathsf{UQMA} \cap \mathsf{co}$-$\mathsf{UQMA}$. These results advance the role of quantum computing in the study of topological phases of matter and provide a pathway for clarifying the connection between topological phases of matter and computational complexity.
Quantum Physics.comment: 38 pages. Accepted for publication in Quantum

Quantum Physics.title: Entanglement and magic transitions in an all-to-all non-Hermitian spin model
Quantum Physics.summary: The long-time state of a non-Hermitian system is determined by the eigenvalue with the largest imaginary part. In interacting many-body systems this eigenvalue usually cannot be tracked analytically, and the character of the state it selects is unknown. We construct a non-Hermitian spin ensemble of $L$ spins with exactly $k$-local all-to-all interactions, in which this dominant eigenvalue can be tracked analytically from the clean limit into the disordered regime. Disorder produces a competition between an isolated spectral outlier and the edge of a many-body spectral bulk. We study three cases: purely anti-Hermitian disorder, purely Hermitian disorder, and mixed disorder of equal strength. For purely anti-Hermitian and mixed disorder, we show that when the bulk overtakes the outlier in imaginary part, the dominant eigenstate switches from an outlier state with low entanglement and magic (nonstabilizerness) to a bulk state with substantially larger entanglement and magic, with both changing at the same threshold. For $k \gg \sqrt{L}$ the bulk has a sharp spectral edge and the transition thresholds follow in closed form, while for $k \ll \sqrt{L}$ spectral tails broaden the transition into a crossover. Purely Hermitian disorder provides a contrasting case with no outlier-to-bulk switching. Finally, we map the non-Hermitian evolution exactly onto postselected trajectories of a monitored quantum system, connecting this spectral mechanism to measurement-induced transitions.

Quantum Physics.title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
Quantum Physics.summary:
Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent.
  To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.

Quantum Physics.title: Multiparticle entanglement in a time-dependent electron--ion--photon system
Quantum Physics.summary: Photoionization provides a natural setting for entanglement transfer in the time domain: an outgoing electron can become entangled with the residual ion, while subsequent spontaneous emission may transfer these correlations to an emitted photon. We quantify the entanglement dynamics of the composite electron--ion--photon system using the von Neumann entropy of the one-versus-rest bipartitions, showing that the initially entangled electron--ion system evolves through a genuinely multiparticle-entangled state before approaching an entangled electron--photon state. Logarithmic negativity further resolves the pairwise entanglement, revealing in particular transient ion--photon entanglement. Further, its enhanced sensitivity to weakly populated Schmidt modes additionally exposes high-dimensional entanglement associated with the photon-energy continuum.

Quantum Physics.title: Coherent-Dissipative Crossover of Quantum Synchronization
Quantum Physics.summary: Quantum synchronization in open systems can arise from both coherent interactions and collective dissipation, yet their interplay remains poorly understood. Here we develop a general framework for two quantum oscillators coupled through a fast mediator. Adiabatic elimination reveals two distinct synchronization channels, coherent exchange and collective dissipation, and yields an analytical description connecting dissipation and coherence-dominated regimes. We show that synchronization is governed by the joint balance of coherent coupling, dissipation, and reservoir-induced fluctuations, rather than by coherent coupling alone. Continuous monitoring of the shared output further converts reservoir information into a resource, substantially enhancing conditional synchronization, with the strongest gain near the coherent-dissipative crossover. These results establish a general mechanism for coherent-dissipative quantum synchronization and its measurement-enabled control in open quantum systems.

Quantum Physics.title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
Quantum Physics.summary: Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold $F=1/2$. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach $N^*=27$ and $N^*=24$ qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.

Quantum Physics.title: Memory of Initial States in Long-Time Dynamics Revealed by Non-Gaussianity
Quantum Physics.summary: In quantum dynamics of few-body observables in quadratic systems, information about the initial state is retained in long-time averages, as captured by the generalized Gibbs ensemble. Here, we show that this memory extends beyond the averages to temporal fluctuations around them. By generating a manifold of non-Gaussian initial states and quantifying their non-Gaussianity via the corresponding entropy, we find that the magnitude of temporal fluctuations is a smooth function of the initial-state non-Gaussianity. This relation explains the qualitatively different scaling of fluctuations observed after quantum quenches: exponentially small fluctuations for non-Gaussian initial states and polynomially small fluctuations for Gaussian initial states. Therefore, our results identify non-Gaussianity as a key to uncovering initial-state memory beyond long-time averages.

Quantum Physics.title: Nonunitary Quantum Criticality Driven by a General Boundary Condition: Exact Solution
Quantum Physics.summary: Nonunitary quantum critical phenomena remain largely unexplored, hindered by the scarcity of exactly solvable models and the numerical challenges in non-Hermitian systems. Here we demonstrate that a general boundary condition drives fundamentally new nonunitary boundary quantum criticality in an exactly solvable lattice model. The exact solution yields a closed-form expression for the boundary-induced equal-time correlation function. The algebraic long-distance behavior of the boundary-induced correlation is governed by the single-particle reflection amplitude at the Fermi level, whose anomalous amplification is forbidden in unitary scattering and therefore provides a direct scattering signature of the nonunitary boundary-critical regime. We use the biorthogonal entanglement entropy as a many-body probe of this boundary-critical behavior and find that it retains logarithmic scaling, while the associated effective central charge, continuously tunable by the boundary parameters, changes from real to complex. The real branch admits a unitary defect conformal field theory (CFT) description, whereas the complex branch lies beyond analytic continuation from the unitary theory. These results establish minimal boundary engineering as an exactly solvable platform for nonunitary boundary quantum criticality and provide a benchmark for broader studies of nonunitary critical phenomena.
Quantum Physics.comment: to be published in Phys. Rev. B. title changed, scattering analysis added

Quantum Physics.title: Two atoms with strong light-induced dipolar interactions
Quantum Physics.summary: We study how two atoms scatter light when they are closer than an optical wavelength and observe multiple new phenomena due to the strong interactions between laser-induced electric dipole moments. We identify a narrow range of densities where a fraction of the scattered light is coherent and shows a collective enhancement factor of two compared to independent atoms. The dynamics of the two-atom wavefunction can be observed through momentum distributions which reveal resonant ejection and depletion. Due to the tight confinement, the total fluorescence intensity strongly depends on the scattering length, since it originates from a narrow resonant (Franck-Condon) region. Furthermore, we measure how the probe laser intensity modifies the scattering length, which establishes a new way to shift Feshbach resonances. Our work provides microscopic insight into what occurs during photoassociation and parity projection in optical tweezers.
Quantum Physics.comment: 10 pages, 7 figures, 8 supplemental figures, 7 pages of supplement

Quantum Physics.title: Dynamical GKP codes
Quantum Physics.summary: Dynamical codes protect quantum information with sequences of measurements, generalizing the stabilizer formalism of static codes. However, the dynamical formalism has been developed exclusively for qubit systems. While Gottesman-Kitaev-Preskill (GKP) codes are promising candidates for quantum computing that encode qubits in the continuous phase space of oscillators, no dynamical formalism has been developed for them. In this work, we bridge this gap and introduce dynamical GKP codes, combining continuous-variable lattice encodings with time-dependent translation measurement dynamics. To obtain the update rules and the distance of a given measurement sequence, we first generalize GKP codes to subsystem GKP codes using scaled symplectic lattices. Building on this structure, we adapt the ancestry, detector, and benign-error machinery originally developed for dynamical qubit codes. From this construction, we obtain a general and efficient method to compute the syndrome and distance of a dynamical GKP code from a persistent stabilizer lattice and a bounded inference window. We illustrate the framework with the example of the two-mode square-hexagonal Floquet GKP code. This code has reduced measurement weight compared to both the square and hexagonal GKP codes, while combining their set of logical gates, resulting in easier implementation of the full single-qubit Clifford group. Finally, we show that measurements with irrational symplectic overlap, which have no analog in discrete qubit codes, reduce to destructive homodyne detection in the single-mode case. These results extend an important qubit-code tool to continuous-variable systems and identify a new bridge between discrete stabilizer measurements and continuous homodyne detection.

Quantum Physics.title: Hidden Coherence and Controlled Quasihole Motion in a Fermionic Laughlin State on a Superconducting Quantum Processor
Quantum Physics.summary: Fractional quantum Hall (FQH) states support fractionalized excitations and geometric phases, yet experimentally resolving the many-body coherence encoded in their wave functions remains challenging. Here, we prepare a three-electron $ν=1/3$ Laughlin state on the Haldane sphere using seven superconducting qubits and reconstruct its many-body density matrix. Through Read's composite-boson construction, we reveal vortex-dressed coherence that remains appreciable over a larger separation range than electron coherence. The extended profile is suppressed in a Fock-diagonal reference constructed from the measured populations, demonstrating its dependence on off-diagonal many-body coherence. We further prepare a one-flux-added quasihole and characterize its fractional charge response against finite-size benchmarks. Controlled quasihole motion yields an effective geometric-phase signature from the reconstructed dominant-eigenstate trajectory. These complementary measurements provide microscopic access to the coherent structure and quasihole response of a finite fermionic Laughlin state, demonstrating an experimental route to probing strongly correlated FQH wave functions on programmable quantum processors.
Quantum Physics.comment: Main text: 8 pages, 4 figures; Supplemental Material: 17 pages, 8 figures

Quantum Physics.title: Parallel and Distributed Fermionic Simulation via Dynamic Encoding
Quantum Physics.summary: We demonstrate a simple and efficient method to parallelize and distribute Trotterized Hamiltonian simulation of fermionic systems across multiple QPUs. Using combinatorial covering designs to define a fixed set of fermion-qubit encodings, independent of system size, we demonstrate communication cost scaling as $\mathcal{O}(M q^3 r)$ for a system of $M$ fermionic modes and Trotter number $r$. This improves on the static encoding bound for $q$ QPUs, $\mathcal{O}(M^4 q r)$. In terms of QPU register size $R$, at most $R^{1/3}$ QPUs are able to parallelize at most $R^{4/3}$ fermionic modes. We compare this approach to dynamic encoding using a randomized method, Pauli-weight based optimization and hypergraph partitioning. Applying these to the Hamiltonians of a range of molecular systems split across two and three QPUs, we find the combinatorial covering approach results in significantly reduced communication cost.

Quantum Physics.title: Semi-device-independent channel identification with communication matrices
Quantum Physics.summary: We look into the task of differentiating between any two quantum channels and reconstructing them from the obtained measurement statistics with possibly limited information about the experimental set-up. We employ the communication matrix formalism where the measurement statistics of a prepare-and-measure scenario is represented as a stochastic communication matrix. In order to differentiate between any two quantum channels, the informational completeness of the set-up is both necessary and sufficient. On the other hand, if we want to uniquely characterize any quantum channel, in addition we also need to have a complete description of the set-up. We show that in many important cases we can deduce this information directly from the communication matrix of the set-up before applying the channel. Given that we trust the dimension of the system, we show that we can deduce the information completeness of the set-up directly from the rank of the communication matrix. Furthermore, we show that another quantity of the communication matrix, called the information storability, can be used to self-test the set-up (up to an orthogonal transformation) for an important class of states and measurements. This provides us a semi-device-independent way to identify quantum channels from the prepare-and-measure statistics. Lastly, we consider scenarios where we might have some additional information about the channels or additional resources at our disposal which could help us relax some of the assumptions of the proposed scenario.
Quantum Physics.comment: 32 pages, 2 figures. Accepted version with minor corrections

Quantum Physics.title: Tunable quantum Mpemba effect in long-range interacting systems
Quantum Physics.summary: Symmetry plays a fundamental role in many-body systems, both in and out of equilibrium. The quantum Mpemba effect (QME) -- a phenomenon where systems initially farther from equilibrium can thermalize faster -- can be understood in terms of how rapidly a symmetry, broken by initial conditions, is dynamically restored. In this work, we study the QME in a one-dimensional spin-1/2 XYZ model with power-law decaying interactions in the presence of a magnetic field. In the prethermal regime generated by large field strengths, the system develops a continuous U(1) symmetry, enabling the QME to emerge. However, due to the Hohenberg-Mermin-Wagner theorem, the QME can only arise when interactions are sufficiently short-ranged. This leads to an interplay between the external field, interaction range, and dynamical symmetry restoration. We systematically explore this interplay and analyze the dependence of the QME on the effective temperature set by the initial state. Our results demonstrate the tunability of the QME via long-range interactions, which can be probed in experimental platforms of trapped ions, polar molecules, and NV centers.

Quantum Physics.title: Fulqrum: a generalized framework for quantum subspace diagonalization
Quantum Physics.summary: We present an open-source software framework for computing the solution to Hamiltonian eigenproblems in a subspace defined by bit-strings sampled from a quantum computer. Hamiltonians are represented using an extended alphabet that includes projection and ladder operators, yielding a unified solution method for qubit and fermionic systems. Operators are grouped and sorted so that only non-zero terms need be evaluated and a minimal number of subspace lookup operations performed. Bit-strings are expressed using bit-sets to reduce memory consumption and allow for evaluating operators with no fundamental limit on the number of qubits. Subspaces defined over bit-sets are stored in a hash map format that allows for efficient indexing and lookup operations. Specializations for problems, such as those from quantum chemistry, can further reduce computational costs. Our method can be used to directly construct sparse matrix Hamiltonian representations or obtain matrix-free solutions, allowing users to utilize their eigensolver of choice. We show the benefits of our framework by computing the ground-state solution to examples from condensed matter physics and quantum chemistry with less memory and runtime compared to existing techniques, in some cases by two orders of magnitude or more. This work provides a flexible interface for performant quantum-classical eigensolutions for candidate quantum advantage applications.

Quantum Physics.title: CV-TF-QKD
Quantum Physics.summary: We introduce a continuous-variable version of twin-field quantum key distribution, using independent Gaussian-modulated coherent states and an untrusted single-photon relay. Full-record reconciliation and a binary phase-disclosure protocol achieve nearly equal asymptotic key rates against collective attacks. At fixed weak input-referred excess noise per arm, both rates per relay use scale as $\sqrtη$, where $η$ is the end-to-end transmissivity. For phase disclosure, we establish composable security against general coherent attacks using a bounded test of preparation intensities and sign-parity complementarity. For specified apparatus parameters, finite-key calculations incorporating detector inefficiency, dark counts, phase fluctuations, and reference overhead predict rates exceeding the pure-loss and matched thermal-loss repeaterless bounds. These results extend the twin-field advantage to Gaussian-modulated continuous-variable quantum cryptography.

Quantum Physics.title: Divergence between Maximum-Probability and Maximum-Likelihood Decoding in the Low-Noise Limit of Quantum Error Correction
Quantum Physics.summary: In the asymptotic low-noise limit of quantum error correction, two optimal decoding rules can disagree. Maximum-probability (MP) decoding selects the most probable microscopic error, whereas degenerate maximum-likelihood (MLD) decoding selects the logical sector with the largest total probability. Under code-capacity Pauli noise, we determine the first physical error weight $m$ at which the MP and MLD logical winner sets become provably disjoint, even under optimal MP tie resolution. As the physical error rate tends to zero, MLD retains a residual zero-temperature degeneracy from the multiplicity of minimum-weight errors sharing a syndrome and logical label, which can outweigh the single most probable error. Code distance imposes the universal bound $m\geq h=\lceil d/2\rceil$; the rigidity depth $r$, defined by $m=h+r$, counts the additional error-weight shells above $h$ on which MP and MLD remain equivalent. We certify a three-level hierarchy: $r=0$ for planar surface codes and two recursively concatenated families, $r=1$ for odd-distance square toric codes and the Gross $[[144,12,12]]$ quantum low-density-parity-check code, and $r=2$ for a separable family with hypergraph product and bivariate bicycle descriptions. The onset weight fixes the leading failure-rate gap between best-tie MP and MLD, proportional to the $m$th power of the physical noise strength, providing an exact subthreshold benchmark for the advantage of degeneracy-aware decoding over the computationally cheaper nondegenerate rule.

Quantum Physics.title: PINNverse meets Jordan--Wigner: learning the Hamiltonian of long spin chains
Quantum Physics.summary: Inverse physics-informed neural networks (PINNverse) learn the parameters of a quantum Hamiltonian from measured expectation values, but the network output grows as $4^N$ with the number of qubits $N$. We show that, for spin chains with nearest-neighbor exchange interactions, the Jordan-Wigner transformation removes this exponential cost: the dynamics closes on an $N\times N$ one-body density matrix, so the network needs only $N^2$ outputs and the data are local observables measured in five global settings. Parasitic $ZZ$ couplings (crosstalk) are included through a time-dependent Hartree--Fock closure. With synthetic data, the same network first solves the equation of motion and then recovers the Hamiltonian parameters of chains of up to $50$ qubits, with couplings learned to better than $0.1\%$. Errors in the local frequencies of long chains are removed by a direct least-squares fit started from the network estimate.

Quantum Physics.title: Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space
Quantum Physics.summary: We present a novel framework to learn a representation of quantum circuits based on the phase space formulation of many-body systems. Given that $N$-qubit states can be represented as probability distributions on a smooth $2N$-dimensional manifold, we show how unitary gates can be parameterized as normalizing flows between these distributions, opening a new avenue for quantum circuit simulation using generative models. We evaluate our method on three common families of quantum circuits, and show that its accuracy exceeds that of current state-of-the-art neural network methods for large system sizes.

Quantum Physics.title: Accelerated spin-adapted ground-state preparation with nonvariational quantum algorithms
Quantum Physics.summary: Various methods have been explored to prepare the spin-adapted ground state, the lowest energy state within the Hilbert space constrained by externally specified values of the total spin magnitude and the spin-$z$ component. In such problem settings, nonvariational methods incorporate penalty terms into the original Hamiltonian to enforce the desired constraints. Such additional terms would require a quartic number of gates in terms of the number $n_{\textrm{spin}}$ of spins when naively implemented. To circumvent this computationally intensive scaling, this paper proposes a new nonvariational procedure to obtain the spin-adapted ground states that requires only quadratic scaling. The proposed method consists of two stages: the first stage is to prepare a spin-magnitude adapted state and the second stage is post-processing for the desired $S_z$. By separating into two stages, the procedure achieves the desired spin-adapted ground state while reducing the number of penalty terms from $O(n_{\textrm{spin}}^4)$ to $O(n_{\textrm{spin}}^2)$. We conducted numerical experiments for spin-1/2 Heisenberg ring models and manganese trimer systems. The results confirmed the effectiveness of our method, demonstrating a significant reduction in gate complexity and validating its practical usefulness.
Quantum Physics.comment: 13 pages, 8 figures; revised following peer review

Quantum Physics.title: Pool-free, residual-triggered ansatz growth for variational imaginary-time evolution: when a fixed operator order beats adaptive screening
Quantum Physics.summary: Adaptive variational algorithms such as ADAPT-VQE and AVQITE screen an operator pool at every growth step, and ADAPT-VQE also re-optimizes all parameters. We study a pool-free alternative for variational imaginary-time evolution (VITE). The layers are fixed in advance by nested commutators of the Hamiltonian, grouped by symmetry and particle number, and the next layer is appended when the relative McLachlan residual exceeds a threshold. On five non-integrable systems (the mixed-field Ising chain and tori, and stretched H$_4$), this dynamic VITE reaches a relative error of $10^{-4}$ with 1.6-5.4 times fewer circuits than the cheapest of six to eight adaptive variants, including single-Pauli-string and qubit-excitation pools and batched ADAPT-VQE. On the chain the advantage persists from 8 to 16 sites. Screening and re-optimization account for most of the adaptive methods' cost. On the spin models, a longitudinal-field scan shows that the advantage requires broken integrability, which makes adaptive screening expensive. The advantage is lost on transverse-field Ising models, at tight targets (relative error $10^{-6}$) and where the schedule front-loads weak layers.

Quantum Physics.title: Millisecond optical coherence and strong collective coupling in an integrated telecom rare-earth photonic platform
Quantum Physics.summary: Long-range quantum network nodes require the combination of strong light-matter coupling, long coherence times and in-situ spectral control at telecom wavelengths. The coherence of erbium in integrated devices is held back by its hosts, which do not simultaneously provide the weakly magnetic nuclear-spin environment and the well-defined substitutional sites found in coherence-optimised bulk crystals. Here we bring such an optimised crystal onto a photonic chip, by bonding an Er${^{3+}}$:CaWO${_{4}}$ host without an adhesive interlayer to a high-${Q}$ electro-optically tuneable thin-film lithium niobate microring resonator. At an effective temperature of 75mK and a field of only 0.2T, ions probed through a waveguide show an effective homogeneous linewidth of ${289\pm5}$Hz (${T_{\text{M}}=1.10\pm0.02}$ms), with spectral diffusion proceeding at ${86\pm18}$Hz and saturating at ${1.5\pm0.2}$kHz. Electro-optically tuning the resonator through the erbium optical transition resolves an avoided crossing with a collective cooperativity of ${C=6.7\pm0.4}$ at zero field and ${C=4.9\pm0.2}$ at 0.4T, where ${T_{\text{M}}}$ exceeds 1ms. Exploiting superhyperfine coupling to the host's ${^{183}}$W nuclear spins, we store and retrieve optical phase information over 5s with a visibility of ${0.935\pm0.015}$. Strong collective coupling, millisecond coherence and in-situ spectral tuning in a single device thus establish heterogeneous integration leveraging coherence-optimised hosts as a route to scalable telecom quantum networks.

Quantum Physics.title: Maximal Violation of Mermin Inequality for Commuting von Neumann Algebras and Multipartite Vacuum Entanglement in QFT
Quantum Physics.summary: Summers and Werner proved that Bell inequalities are violated maximally and generically in the vacuum of a relativistic quantum field theory in [S. J. Summers and R. Werner, Commun. Math. Phys. 110 (1987), 247-259]. Their criterion concerns two-party case, that is, there are two algebras of quantum observables: one algebra and its commutant. In this case, the maximal CHSH value is converged to in every normal state exactly when the algebra is strongly stable. In the paper, we study the corresponding question for three and more mutually commuting von Neumann algebras. We focus on the multipartite Mermin inequalities instead of CHSH ones. For the tripartite Mermin functional we show that maximal violation in every normal state is equivalent to the existence of a common sequence of asymptotic GHZ stabilizers. Strong stability of each local factor is an necessary condition for maximal violation, and a joint embedding of an infinite GHZ tensor product is sufficient. Counterexamples show that strong stability and type III_1 of the individual algebras, even together with tripartite duality, do not suffice to arrive at the maximal violation. The results are also extended to n>=3 parties.

Quantum Physics.title: Quantum Simulation of Quantum Channels and Applications
Quantum Physics.summary: We review the basic theory of quantum channels and develop a strategy for simulating them on digital quantum computers, drawing upon the Choi-Kraus operator-sum representation and Stinespring dilation to provide a unified approach for various applications. We discuss three types of applications, offering explicit examples for each: the preparation of mixed states, measurements described by positive operator-valued measures (POVMs), and the simulation of the evolution of Markovian quantum systems. We recover fundamental concepts from quantum theory, such as the purification of a mixed state and the Naimark dilation associated with a POVM. Regarding the simulation of the evolution of a Markovian quantum system, we introduce an operator, termed the residual operator, to construct, from the system's Liouvillian, a quantum channel that serves as a first-order approximation of the quantum dynamical semigroup. This allows the simulation of quantum dynamics to be performed in a manner analogous to the Euler method for ordinary differential equations, avoiding Trotterization. We prove all the theoretical results mentioned, with the exception of the fundamental Choi-Kraus theorem concerning the operator-sum representation of quantum channels, for which we provide the appropriate references. The explicit simulations discussed were implemented using the AerSimulator from IBM's Qiskit SDK, with the corresponding code available on GitHub.

Quantum Physics.title: Quantum propagation of vibrational excitation in harmonically confined trapped-ion crystal
Quantum Physics.summary: Vibrational excitations, or phonons, in trapped ions serve as useful resources for quantum information processing, including quantum simulation and computing. Localized excitations of ions' vibrational motion (local phonons) can be used for simulating quantum particles that propagate over a system. Here, we experimentally investigate the propagation of a localized vibrational excitation in a one-dimensional trapped-ion crystal. A 10-ion crystal confined in a harmonic potential is used. It is found that inhomogeneity in the spacing between the ions leads to characteristic behaviors such as adjacent hopping and global movement. A comparison of the experimental results with numerical simulations shows agreement up to fine details. The system explored here may be extended to many-body systems of bosonic particles as well as more complex quasiparticles.

Quantum Physics.title: Single-molecule strong optomechanical regimes in SERS via hybrid plasmonic cavities
Quantum Physics.summary: We identify enhanced strong coherent Surface-Enhanced Raman Scattering (SERS) interactions facilitated by hybridized metallo-dielectric cavities with a resonant fluorescent molecule. By illuminating a detuned electronic transition near saturation via a narrowband hybrid plasmonic mode, we observe enhanced splittings in the Stokes and anti-Stokes spectra, revealing strong optomechanical coupling and nonlinear vibrational modifications at intensities far below irreversible SERS damage thresholds. We compute the second-order photon correlations that allows identifying the nonclassical character associated to these strong optomechanical interactions and SERS configurations that enables them to optically characterize the anharmonic character of the vibrational modes.

Quantum Physics.title: How many degrees of freedom describe a quantum N-particle state?
Quantum Physics.summary: In Newtonian spacetime, the canonical description of a classical $N$-particle system requires $3N$ degrees of freedom. Not all of these are physical, however, since the conservation of the net momentum implies that only $3(N-1)$ accelerations are independent. Hence, three constraints can be used to eliminate the unphysical centre-of-mass variables, at the level of the Lagrangian, leaving only the subset of observable displacements and momenta, which are relational. Imposing the constraints does not change the dynamics of these variables, at the classical level, and is analogous to a gauge-fixing procedure, which removes redundancy in the description of the system. In classical physics, therefore, the number of physical degrees of freedom equals the number of independent relational degrees of freedom. Here, we show that this is not the case in quantum mechanics. While an operator-analogue of the classical net momentum exists, it cannot be used to impose constraints that restrict the degrees of freedom in the theory, without a loss of physical information. This means that all $3N$ canonical degrees of freedom are physical, even though only $3(N-1)$ of them are relational. We explore the physical consequences of the non-relational variables and show that they give rise to generalised uncertainty relations (GURs), for the relational quantities that define the quantum reference frame (QRF). Hence, it is shown that the non-relational degrees of freedom refer to the frame itself and that the non-Heisenberg terms in the GURs define its Galilean-invariant spreads, in both real space and momentum space. The implications of this result for recent work on relational models, including the ``perspective neutral'' framework for QRFs, are discussed. Its implications for the wider relational program, and, in particular, the relevance of the latter to quantum gravity research, are also critically assessed
Quantum Physics.comment: 35 pages of main text, 25 pages of appendices, and 9 pages of references. No tables, no figures. Accepted for publication in Classical and Quantum Gravity

Quantum Physics.title: Multiparameter quantum estimation of circulant networks
Quantum Physics.summary: Networks provide a natural description of interaction patterns, transport media, and communication architectures. Accurately characterizing their coupling structure is a key challenge in quantum technologies. We investigate the multiparameter quantum estimation of coupling strengths in circulant networks probed by continuous-time quantum walks. We derive the quantum Fisher information matrix, identify the optimal probe states and determine the ultimate precision allowed by quantum measurements, together with its scaling with the number of unknown couplings. We further analyze the precision achievable through position measurements of the walker, comparing the corresponding classical Cramér-Rao bounds for optimal and localized probe states with the quantum limit. Finally, we consider finite-resolution detection modeled by coarse-grained position measurements. Although coarse graining generally reduces estimation precision, we find that lower-resolution measurements can, in some instances, outperform other measurements with finer spatial resolution. Our results provide a systematic characterization of the fundamental and practical limits of coupling estimation in quantum-walk-based network inference.

Quantum Physics.title: CV-QKD over Turbulence Channels with Virtual Photon Subtraction and Quantum Multiple-Symbol Detection for Underwater Quantum Communications
Quantum Physics.summary: Continuous-variable quantum key distribution (CV-QKD) is a promising approach for secure underwater quantum communications (UQCs), where propagation loss, scattering, turbulence, and receiver thermal noise can severely degrade the transmission of quantum states. In this paper, we propose an underwater CV-QKD system with virtual photon subtraction (VPS), implemented through post-selection of Alice's measurement outcomes, without requiring channel state information (CSI) at the receiver. Three VPS-based system configurations are analyzed, corresponding to homodyne detection (VPS-HD), quantum maximum-likelihood detection (VPS-QMLD), and quantum multiple-symbol detection (VPS-QMSD). System performance is evaluated in terms of the accepted-only quantum bit error rate (QBER), where underwater turbulence is modeled by an Erlang distribution. Analytical and semi-closed-form QBER expressions are derived for the three configurations and validated through Monte Carlo simulations for different water types and system parameters. The results show close agreement between analytical and simulation results and demonstrate that VPS-QMSD provides the best robustness against underwater turbulence, achieving the lowest QBER compared with VPS-QMLD and VPS-HD.

Quantum Physics.title: Reservoir-induced Quantum Phase Transitions in spin ensembles
Quantum Physics.summary: In this work, we present a comprehensive analysis of an open quantum system consisting of a collection of N two-level atoms in the thermodynamic limit coupled to bosonic reservoirs. Our results demonstrate that, when the system-bath interactions lacks a metastable minimum, as in the counterterm-free case, the system can undergo a quantum phase transition set by the reservoir structure rather than by coherent internal dynamics. Using exact quantum Langevin equations, valid even in the overdamped regime near criticality, where the loss rates can exceed the resonance frequency of the softening mode, we locate the critical point via the complex excitation spectrum and obtain closed-form reflection and transmission spectra that display the mode softening and an increasingly asymmetric lineshape near the transition.

Quantum Physics.title: Programmable quantum simulation of anharmonic dynamics
Quantum Physics.summary: In continuous-variable quantum systems, anharmonicity underlies diverse processes such as proton transfer, false vacuum decay and ferroelectric ordering, which cannot arise in a purely harmonic potential. Here, we experimentally demonstrate trigonometric-gate-implemented Fourier synthesis (TGIFS), a compilation scheme for quantum simulation of anharmonic dynamics in continuous-variable-discrete-variable (CV-DV) quantum simulators. TGIFS uses native CV-DV gates, allowing a target anharmonic potential to be determined entirely by classical control parameters, without modification of the hardware. We programmably implement TGIFS with a single trapped ion, simulating coherent dynamics in a continuously tunable family of double-well potentials and synthesising a quartic phase gate. The same circuit structure extends to arbitrary potentials and to multiple modes, giving a route to universal programmable simulation of nonlinearly coupled anharmonic potentials as achievable circuit depth increases.

Quantum Physics.title: Causal Order Cannot Be An Observable
Quantum Physics.summary:
Recent developments in the formalisation of quantum causal structures have made it possible to test and compare hypotheses about causal structure empirically, rather than being a-priori assumptions. Such differences in causal structure may be leveraged to distinguish between the processes they belong to, akin to distinguishing between quantum states known to belong to different eigenspaces of an observable. So how far this analogy can be pushed? Can causal order be interpreted as a kind of observable? Can it be measured?
  To this end we construct a completely operational definition of observables in terms of `discrimination tasks'. This begins with some base set of classes (analogous to a quantum observable's eigenspaces) before we impose three conditions on how these classes relate under discrimination tasks. These conditions recover the properties of a standard observable, letting us apply this definition to non-state entities such as quantum processes, which naturally encode causal structure.
  The first of these conditions (1) asserts that a member of any class is perfectly distinguishable from a member of any other class -- for states, this implies conditions (2) and (3), but we show this does not hold automatically for processes (or indeed channels). By analysing classes of quantum processes having strict causal orders, we find causal classes which are sharp but violate condition 2 (but not 3), and classes which are likewise sharp and violate condition 3 (but not 2). This implies that causal order cannot be an observable.

Quantum Physics.title: QuantumBilliards.jl: An extensible, user friendly, high-performance Julia library for the large scale computation of spectra and eigenstates of quantum billiards and related problems
Quantum Physics.summary:
